take: The Houthi missile and drone strike on the Saudi tanker Amzan off Yanbu, alongside Washington's expanded "economic asphyxiation" campaign against Iran, is the key crude story today, reigniting supply risk premia in the Red Sea and Gulf even as Brent pulls back on profit-taking. This geopolitical heat directly supports product cracks, particularly for middle distillates, whilst the threat to Saudi west-coast exports via Yanbu adds a fresh logistical wrinkle to an already tight Atlantic Basin barrel. In freight, the sinking of the panamax bulker Ocean Winner in the Bay of Bengal with 22 crew missing and the Amazon drought-driven container surcharges of up to $1,900 highlight escalating operational risks and tonne-mile inflation across dry bulk and container, which will feed into higher delivered costs for energy commodities. The flow angle is defensive: the lack of major Chinese banks in the new Iran sanctions removes a key escalation risk, but the market is still pricing a higher floor under Iranian supply disruption, whilst Nigeria's seven-fold surge in seaborne product exports since 2023, driven by Dangote, continues to normalise Atlantic Basin gasoline and gasoil balances. Watch for further Houthi escalation headlines and any confirmation of damage to the Amzan, which would spike VLCC and Suezmax rates on the Saudi west coast and widen Brent-Dubai spreads in the next 24 hours.

items.title: Dangote refinery drives increase in petroleum shipments from Nigeria

items.summary: Well operators in the Permian region of western Texas and eastern New Mexico are getting more oil and gas out of the ground by drilling longer, horizontal wells and increasingly incorporating so-called super-lateral wells that exceed 15,000 feet.

items.title: Waterborne shipments from the U.S. Gulf Coast increased in April and May

Shipments from the U.S. Gulf Coast to the East Coast (PADD 1) also increased.
